title: Global Ethanol Outlook 2026 | BloombergNEF
gist: BNEF expects road-transport ethanol demand to peak at 2.4 million b/d in 2031 and roughly halve by 2050 as EVs displace conventional fuels, freeing over 1.2 million b/d for shipping and aviation — though EU rules restricting crop-based feedstocks limit how much existing corn/sugarcane ethanol qualifies. US (51%) and Brazil (27%) dominate supply, US exports are rising, and India has become the third-largest producer.

insights.claim: In BNEF's Economic Transition Scenario, global ethanol demand in road transport peaks at 2.4 million barrels per day (139 billion liters a year) in 2031.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: Ethanol producers face a structural demand ceiling within roughly five years; long-dated capacity investment tied to gasoline blending carries terminal-demand risk.
insights.locator: Outlook: Ethanol demand in road transport

insights.claim: Because ethanol demand is tied to conventional road-fuel consumption, rising electric-vehicle adoption drives road-transport ethanol demand down by around 50% between 2031 and 2050 in BNEF modeling.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: EV penetration is the key variable for ethanol volumes; track EV adoption as a leading indicator for corn/sugarcane ethanol demand.
insights.quote: Ethanol demand is therefore linked with the consumption of conventional road fuels, which in BloombergNEF modeling peaks in 2031 and then falls by around half as electric-vehicle adoption rises.
insights.locator: Ethanol is widely consumed as a road fuel

insights.claim: The post-2031 decline in road-fuel ethanol demand leaves more than 1.2 million barrels per day (71 billion liters a year) of ethanol supply available for other uses by 2050.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: A large stranded-supply overhang could pressure ethanol prices unless new end markets absorb it.
insights.locator: Outlook: Ethanol demand in road transport

insights.claim: Surplus ethanol freed by falling road-fuel demand could be redirected to harder-to-abate transport sectors such as shipping and aviation.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: Ethanol-to-jet and marine-fuel pathways are the potential demand backstop for ethanol producers; watch offtakes and policy support in these segments.

insights.claim: Demand-side policies, particularly in the EU, restrict crop-based feedstocks, limiting the share of existing ethanol supply (largely corn and sugarcane based) that qualifies for shipping and aviation decarbonization uses.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: Crop-based ethanol may not capture the new decarbonization demand in regulated markets like the EU, so the surplus may not be cleanly absorbed — a headwind for US corn and Brazilian sugarcane ethanol.

themes.theme: Supply concentration in US and Brazil

insights.claim: The US and Brazil accounted for 51% and 27% of global ethanol production respectively in 2025, remaining the dominant producers.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: Nearly four-fifths of global ethanol supply sits in two countries, so US and Brazilian policy and crop conditions drive global ethanol balances.

insights.claim: Almost all US ethanol is produced from corn, while Brazilian ethanol relies significantly on sugarcane.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: US ethanol is directly exposed to crop-based feedstock restrictions and links ethanol demand to corn markets.

insights.claim: US ethanol exports have risen over the past three years, reaching 13% of US production in 2025, supported by importing markets seeking to cut transport emissions and reliance on imported crude and refined products.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: Export demand is a growing outlet for US ethanol producers and partly offsets domestic road-fuel saturation.

insights.claim: India raised its ethanol blending rate to 20% in 2025 from 2% in 2017 and is now the world's third-largest ethanol producer.
insights.speaker: Jade Patterson
insights.so_what: India is the fastest-growing developing ethanol market; its blending policy is a key swing factor for global demand and sugar/grain feedstock markets.
